cells.tense: You are finishing something in the presence of the people it touched, and you know it is finishing.
cells.ask: Tell the people involved that this chapter is done. Then leave one thing about it genuinely open, so whatever comes next has a door.
cells.core:
Something you were part of is coming to its end and you're right there for it. Not holding on, not walking out early — you're in the middle of the people it involved and it's wrapping up in front of you. The ones on the far end of these ties can feel that you know when a thing is finished.

That's the whole of it. You can close something without sealing it. What you're carrying is the ease of someone who has done this before and isn't scared of the ending. Keep that. The only thing worth feeding now is what's already walking toward you — an invitation will come, and you get to choose it fresh, without dragging the last room behind you. The ease is real. Just don't leave before it's actually finished.
cells.sheetLine: You can close a chapter without sealing the door.
cells.verb: bringing a thing to the point where it can be let go
cells.place: in the ties that hold you and the people on the other end of them

cells.tense: You are bracing for the ending to land before it has actually arrived.
cells.ask: Pick one unfinished thing and let it stay visibly unfinished this week — no summary, no verdict, no announcement that it's over.
cells.core:
You keep declaring things finished before they are. Someone says something and you're already writing the ending for it, already counting it as over, already somewhere past a place you haven't actually arrived at yet. The people around you can feel the hurry, and it's closing things that still had room to breathe.

What you're reaching for is real — you want the clean finish, the part where it's done and you can move. But you're calling it early, and the early call is costing you the people who are still in the middle of it with you. Close what's closed. Let the rest stay open a little longer than feels safe. The truth of where a thing actually is won't arrive any slower than it does.
cells.sheetLine: You're calling it finished before it is.
cells.verb: bringing a thing to the point where it can be let go
cells.place: in the ties that hold you and the people on the other end of them

cells.tense: You have been waiting at a door that already closed behind you, and still treating it as open.
cells.ask: Name one thing that ended. Say it out loud once, to yourself or to someone, and don't soften it.
cells.core:
There's something behind you that's already done, and you're still treating it like it's the one you're waiting on. So nothing new gets to count. You hold something open that wants to close, and holding it open looks like seeking — like the next thing is coming, like you're still in the middle of choosing. Meanwhile the people in front of you can't quite reach you, because part of you is somewhere back at a door that's shut.

Being with someone who is actually here — that's what's starved, not the pull toward the next thing. Warmth into other people's hands is what pulls it back, not more pressure on yourself to feel something you can't currently reach. One thing that ended, said plainly. That's the whole ask. The room you're standing in is real. Answer what's in it.
cells.sheetLine: Something is over. You're still calling it pending.
cells.verb: bringing a thing to the point where it can be let go
cells.place: in the ties that hold you and the people on the other end of them

cells.tense: You are letting go of things you have not yet admitted were complete, and calling it something else.
cells.ask: Write down one thing you've already stopped carrying, and mark the date it stopped, if you can remember one.
cells.core:
By the time most things end, you've already set them down and you didn't notice doing it. That's not neglect — it's how you release, quietly and earlier than you say. What's missing is the catching of it. You talk about a few things as if they're still open, still yours to settle, and by the record of your own days they aren't.

The release already happened. You just haven't put words to it. You don't have to announce a loss to name what's passed — it's admitting the hand is already empty and has been for a while. What you're feeling isn't a departure; it's the ordinary tidying that comes after finishing. Look at one thing you're calling unfinished and check whether you actually still hold it.
cells.sheetLine: You already let go. You're still calling it unfinished.
cells.verb: bringing a thing to the point where it can be let go
cells.place: in the ties that hold you and the people on the other end of them

attempts.check: Unsupported claim: that the person is tied to a specific earlier cycle that has ended without their naming it — Too Little may locate them behind the present, but the record does not say what happened there or when. A reader could reasonably say the endless seeking is their temperament, not a stalled ending, and my Too Little wording must survive that. The asks stay useful if I'm wrong: naming an ending once, or bringing one thing all the way to done, teaches something about their own pace either way. The sentence that serves me more than them is any line about turning points and fresh entry — it belongs to the card, not their life, so it stays off the page except as their own plain words.
